newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: EU's Brittan wants new trade talks for new century.
newsitem.headline: EU's Brittan wants new trade talks for new century.

text.p: The European Union, Britain and Australia urged fellow members of the body that makes rules on international trade on Monday to set the goal of a new global round of trade talks to usher in the 21st century.
European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan proposed calling the talks the "Millennium Round".

Many countries are cool about launching fresh multilateral trade negotiations so soon after the completion in 1994 of the Uruguay Round of talks, which opened up markets in goods, services, farm produce, textiles and intellectual property.
Developing countries in particular say they need more time to make the wrenching economic changes required of them.

The United States, too, is concerned that the prospect of a new multilateral round of talks would give governments an excuse to play for time in pressing negotiations to liberalise specific sectors, such as telecommunications and financial services.

Brittan, acknowledging those concerns, said the Commission, the Brussels-based executive of the European Union, was not looking for immediate long-term commitments to liberalisation at this week's meeting of the World Trade Organisation.

"A work programme does not prejudge any possible future decision to move to negotiations. This will be for us all to take freely, later," he told the opening session of the WTO's first ministerial conference.

"But this week's decisions should make it possible for us to launch in due course the further broad-based round of talks, which could properly be called the Millennium Round, that I personally believe can start by the end of the century.
"That is not something to decide today. But in all our decisions here in Singapore, we should prepare ourselves so that WTO is ready to take up that challenge in the years ahead," he added.
Britain's trade and industry secretary, Ian Lang, backed Brittan, saying global free trade was a recipe for faster economic growth and rising living standards.
Lang said he sympathised with those countries that say they have enough on their plate digesting the Uruguay Round.
"But I have to say that that is not enough. We must drive the agenda forward: we will all gain in the long term," he said.

In a speech to ministers, Lang proposed that the WTO should next tackle the issues of government procurement, investment and cutting through red tape binding exporters and importers as a prelude to the next conference of WTO ministers in 1998.
They in turn would pave the way for the launch of a new multilateral trading round before the end of the century with the goal of delivering a big package of liberalisation measures before 2010.
Australia's deputy prime minister, Tim Fischer, welcomed Brittan's call, but Lang acknowledged at a news conference that views within the 15-member European Union were mixed.
"It's not an issue that has been directly addressed," Lang said.

He said a new trade round would set the stage for an even more ambitious goal of global free trade by 2020 -- a regional aim reaffirmed last month by the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.
"If the whole of APEC can set itself a target for free trade by 2020, why cannot the WTO do the same? Lang asked.
